findings.where: Screens 3, 5 and 7, with the readouts on screens 2, 4 and 6
findings.what: Each typed answer is printed in a readout on the screen just before it, so Dan can recall it or press Back instead of working it: screen 2 ends on Output 110.35 V and Regulation 4.0% (the answers to screens 3 and 5), screen 4 opens on 4.0% at unity, and screen 6 ends on −0.5% at 0.5 leading (the answer to screen 7). Hide the Output and Regulation readouts on screen 2, and the Regulation readout on screen 4's opening and on screen 6.

The answer is graded to ±0.005 V (110.35 V) but the question never asks for two decimal places, and 110.4 V, the figure the Practice worked example gives for this same case, gets only the generic triangle hint. Add "to two decimal places" to the question, or add 110.4 as a slip whose hint asks for the triangle worked to 0.01 V.

findings.where: Screen 10, "So a short at the terminals draws 1739 A"
findings.what: The sentence is stated flat, but 1739 A holds only with a stiff supply, and a real supply and its cables make the fault smaller. The brief promised the screen would say so. Write "With a stiff supply, a short at the terminals draws 1739 A", which brings the screen to 88 words.

"Its drop starts from a no-load voltage set by the turns ratio. So a leading load can lift its output above that" is offered as a difference, but a cable shares it: the same r cos φ + x sin φ sum with a leading load can lift a cable's far end above its sending voltage. Drop these two sentences, or replace them with a real difference, such as the transformer's R and X coming from its own tests and plate.

findings.where: Screen 5, the hint for the 5.0 slip
findings.what: "At unity most of the reactance drop points across" is wrong: at unity all of the I × X drop is at right angles to the output. Say "At unity the reactance drop points straight across, so it costs almost nothing."

findings.where: Screens 2 to 9, the readouts and the fault bar
findings.what: The Regulation readout appears on screen 2, before screen 4 defines the term. The Fault current bar and readout sit on every screen from screen 2, fixed at 1739 A, and are not explained until screen 10. Show each one only from the screen that introduces it.

At 9 units a volt, the 0.55 V by which the output passes the No load mark at 0.5 leading is about 4 px on a 360 px phone, so the lesson's most surprising result is almost invisible, and the full-load drop triangle is only about 44 px across. Zoom the drawing further (the axis spends 95 to 105 V on nothing), or add an inset around the tip.

Two short steps are skipped. The parts along the output are IR cos φ and IX sin φ because the I × R arrow sits at φ to the output and the I × X arrow a quarter-turn further on. The full-load copper loss share equals R% because I²R ÷ VI = IR ÷ V. Add one sentence each, and trim elsewhere to stay under 90 words.
"At this load, 0.8 lagging gives the deepest sag" ties the worst angle to the load, but the windings' own angle sets it at any load. Say "For this transformer, 0.8 lagging gives the deepest sag."

No screen asks Dan to predict before a demonstration plays, though the brief promised a prediction in every lesson, so every DO screen asks back a figure its SHOW screen has just given. A one-tap prediction before screen 6 would make the leading surprise land harder, for example "Will 0.8 leading sag more or less than unity?"

Screen 10's impedance slider snaps to 4%, and its demonstration passes through 4% showing 2174 A, which is screen 11's answer. Ask screen 11 about a unit not on the slider, for example 20 kVA at 115 V and 4%, which gives 173.9 × 25 = 4348 A.

findings.where: Screens 4, 6 and 8, the power factor buttons at 360 px
findings.what: The seven buttons fall into rows of 3, 3 and 1, with "0.5 lead" alone on a third row, not the 4 and 3 the stylesheet comment intends. Lower the grid minimum from 4.4rem to about 3.9rem.
At 90 words it sits at the ceiling and runs to 15 lines at 360 px. "Here is last lesson's transformer, seen from its 115 V side" repeats the caption and could go.
"What do you get?" is vague for a list of statements to judge. "Which is true of the two?" asks what is meant.
"A 2.5% unit of the same size sags only 2.5% at 0.8 lagging" holds only if it keeps the same 4 to 3 split of R and X, so say so.
"Read ... the impedance, Z%, from the plate" should name what Dan will actually see there, the impedance voltage or Usc, so he recognises it on a job, as the brief planned.
